body.heading: A number too big to picture
paragraphs: The odds of winning the Powerball jackpot with one ticket are about 1 in 292 million. Numbers that size slide off the brain, so translate it. Winning is roughly as likely as flipping a coin and getting heads 28 times in a row - every single flip landing the same way, no mistakes allowed.

Or try this: imagine one particular second picked at random from a span of more than nine years, and trying to name it exactly on your first guess. That is the size of the target a single ticket is aiming at.

body.heading: Why more tickets barely help
paragraphs: Buying 100 tickets sounds like a strategy, but it only changes your odds to about 100 in 292 million. You have spent a hundred times more money to move from 'almost impossible' to 'still almost impossible'. The maths of the jackpot is not really about the number of tickets; it is about the size of the denominator.

There is also a quieter calculation called expected value: on average, a ticket returns only a fraction of its price, because most of the prize pool is concentrated in a jackpot almost nobody wins. That does not make a ticket a crime - plenty of people buy one for the fun of imagining - but it does mean the imagination is the product you are really purchasing.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Practise feeling smaller odds first. Guessing a friend's four-digit PIN on the first try is 1 in 10,000. Guessing the exact minute of the day someone was born is about 1 in 1,440. Notice how even these feel hopeless - then remember the jackpot is hundreds of thousands of times less likely than the PIN.

For a fairer game, design a classroom raffle: 200 tickets, one prize. Now the odds are 1 in 200 - small enough to be exciting, big enough that somebody in the room plausibly wins. Good game design lives at that human scale.

takeaway: Huge odds get clearer with comparisons: a jackpot ticket is roughly as likely to win as flipping a coin to heads 28 times straight.
